{{nihongo|'''Wakenosu Shrine'''|和気能須命神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in Shimonishi, {{ill|Okinoshima, Shimane|arz|اوكينوشيما|ceb|Okinoshima Chō|de|Okinoshima (Shimane)|es|Okinoshima (Shimane)|fa|اوکینوشیما، شیمانه|fr|Okinoshima|id|Okinoshima, Shimane|it|Okinoshima|ja|隠岐の島町|ko|오키노시마정|ms|Okinoshima, Shimane|my|အိုခိနိုရှိမမြို့၊ ရှိမနဲ|pl|Okinoshima|ru|Окиносима|sv|Okinoshima, Shimane|tl|Okinoshima, Shimane|tr|Okinoshima|ur|اوکینوشیما، شیمانے|zh|隱岐之島町|qid=Q1205039}}, {{ill|Oki District, Shimane|Q735735|qid=Q735735}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|Q132751|qid=Q132751}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|lt=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} (minor shrine), and its former shrine rank was village shrine. Its common name is '''Matsuo Shrine'''. {{nihongo|'''Wakenosu Shrine'''|和気能須命神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Oki Province]].

== Overview ==
The year of enshrinement is unknown, but it is identified as the shrine corresponding to “Wakenosu-no-Mikoto Shrine” listed in the *{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}*{{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=495}}. In the *{{ill|Izumi Province Divine Name Register|ja|国内神名帳|qid=Q11420490|lt=Oshu Jinmyōchō}}*, it is recorded as the collective shrine of Shimonishi under the name “Junior First Rank Wakenosu Ōmyōjin”{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=979}}{{efn|This “Junior First Rank” is thought to refer to a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Sōgen Senji}} decree{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}.}}. In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} 5 (1872), it was ranked as a village shrine{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}.

Commonly called “Matsuo Shrine,” it is known as a deity of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sake brewing}} {{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=495}}{{efn|Because the mountain stream flowing beside the shrine precincts provided high-quality water suitable for brewing sake, the name was written as “Wakenosake.” It is also said that in the medieval period, {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|de|Matsunoo-Schrein|fr|Matsunoo-taisha|it|Santuario Matsunoo|ja|松尾大社|my|မဆွတ်နိုအိုတိုင်းရှ|ru|Мацуноо-тайся|zh|松尾大社|qid=Q710302|lt=Matsuo Myōjin}} was invited from {{ill|Yamashiro Province|Q749276|qid=Q749276}}{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=979}}. There is also a theory that it came to be regarded as a deity of sake brewing only after the name began to be written as “Wakenosake”{{sfn|Rikabi-no-ya|1987c|p=293}}.}}. The shrine crest is a “gourd within a circle”{{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=494}}.

== Enshrined Deity ==
'''Wakenosu-no-Mikoto''' (わけのすのみこと)

This deity is thought to be related to Mizuwakasu-no-Mikoto of {{ill|Mizuwakasu Shrine|Q11549109|qid=Q11549109}} and Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto of {{ill|Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto Shrine|ja|玉若酢命神社|qid=Q11572773}}. While the divine nature is unclear, there are two major views: one that considers the deity a personal god, and another that sees it as a nature god{{sfn|Rikabi-no-ya|1987a|p=184}}.

* Personal Deity Theory  
: This view is typified by an essay included in *Shimane Prefectural History* by Shimizu Shinzaburō{{sfn|Shimizu|1923}}{{sfn|Rikabi-no-ya|1987a|p=184}}{{sfn|Rikabi-no-ya|1987b|p=256}}. Shimizu regarded “mizu (water) = mizu (auspicious)” and “tama (jewel)” as honorific expressions, and assumed a blood relationship between the two Wakasu deities{{sfn|Shimizu|1923|p=227}}. He then argued: “1. During the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723|lt=Keikō}}, imperial relatives were distributed across various provinces and so-called ‘branch’ administrations were established”{{sfn|Shimizu|1923|pp=228–229}}; “2. The fifth imperial prince of Keikō, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōsu-wake no Ōji}}, seems to have been assigned to Oki as a ‘branch’ and governed there”{{sfn|Shimizu|1923|pp=229–230}}; “3. Wakenosu-no-Mikoto Shrine likely enshrines Ōsu-wake-no-Mikoto”{{sfn|Shimizu|1923|pp=230–232}}. From this, he inferred that Mizuwakasu-no-Mikoto and Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto, whose ancestral shrine was Wakenosu-no-Mikoto Shrine, divided and governed {{ill|Dōgojima|be|Догадзіма|bg|Дого (Шимане)|ceb|Dōgo|de|Dōgo|fr|Dōgo-jima|id|Dōgojima|ja|島後|ko|도고섬|ru|Дого (остров)|sv|Dogo|zh|島後|qid=Q3623017}}{{sfn|Shimizu|1923|p=231}}. In other words, this theory identifies the enshrined deity '''Wakenosu-no-Mikoto with Prince Ōsu-wake'''.

* Nature Deity Theory  
: This view is represented by Shiga Tsuyoshi’s *Studies on Shikinaisha*{{sfn|Shiga|1981}}{{sfn|Rikabi-no-ya|1987a|p=184}}. Shiga considered Wakenosu-no-Mikoto to be a shortened form of “Wakenowakasu-no-Mikoto,” with the “waka” omitted, and regarded the shrine as corresponding to a subsidiary shrine of Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto Shrine{{sfn|Shiga|1981|p=558}}. As for the divine nature, he inferred it to be '''a deity who causes the water of a pond beside the shrine to spring forth'''{{sfn|Shiga|1981|p=558}}. He further interpreted Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto as meaning “causing jeweled water to spring forth,” based on the exceptionally pure groundwater of Shimonishi Village where Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto Shrine is located{{sfn|Shiga|1981|p=557}}; and Mizuwakasu-no-Mikoto as a deity who causes pure water to spring forth (“Mizu-wakasu-no-Mikoto”), focusing on the Yamada River flowing through Yamada, the former shrine site of Mizuwakasu Shrine, and the place name {{ill|Ochi district|ja|穏地郡|zh|穩地郡|qid=Q11597172|lt=Ochi}} meaning “rejuvenating water”{{sfn|Shiga|1981|p=561}}. While he considered Tamawakasu-no-Mikoto Shrine and Mizuwakasu Shrine to be symmetrical, he did not posit a direct relationship among the enshrined deities of these three shrines{{sfn|Shiga|pp=557, 560}}.

== Facilities ==
;Main Hall  
: A modified {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|Q3193781|qid=Q3193781}}{{efn|Some sources describe it as {{ill|Oki-zukuri|Q11659055|qid=Q11659055}}{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}.}}, measuring 1 ken in width and 1.3 ken in depth{{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=495}}. The erection of the main hall’s pillars is thought to date to {{ill|Kansei|Q1195131|qid=Q1195131}} 2 (1790){{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}.
;Connecting Hall  
: {{ill|Kirizuma-style|Q13308575|qid=Q13308575}}{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}, measuring 1.3 ken in width and 2.3 ken in depth{{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=495}}.
;Worship Hall  
: {{ill|East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Q855025|qid=Q855025}}{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}, measuring 2.1 ken in width and 2.1 ken in depth{{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=495}}.
;Pilgrims’ Lodging{{sfn|Takahashi et al., eds.|1996|p=495}}  
: In Oki, there was a custom called “okomori,” in which people would pray at their tutelary shrine for recovery from illness, safe childbirth, abundant catches, or school admission, and then, as thanks for fulfillment, spend a night secluded in a hut called “komosha” or “komoriya” located within the shrine precincts{{sfn|Ōtsu|1973|p=310}}.
;Torii  
: Myōjin-style torii{{sfn|Handa|1983|p=980}}.
